claim: Industry fees, not taxpayer appropriations, cover most of the U.S. Food and Drug Administration's prescription-drug review costs. Under the Prescription Drug User Fee Act (PDUFA) — the 1992 law that lets the FDA charge drugmakers fees to review their applications — pharmaceutical-company user fees covered 77% of the PDUFA program's total costs in fiscal year 2025, with congressional appropriations covering the remaining 23%. When the program began in fiscal year 1993, user fees covered just 7%.

sources.label: Congressional Research Service, 'FDA Human Medical Product User Fee Programs' (R44750)
sources.quote: in FY2025 (from the most recent financial report available), user fees covered 77% of PDUFA program total costs (nonuser fee appropriations covered 23%).

sources.label: Cole Soiney / @rant.board, Instagram reel DZJJvUbtJ2g (June 3, 2026) — surfacing source

notes: The reel's '77% of the drug reviews' is accurate for the PDUFA prescription-drug review program specifically (FY2025, per CRS citing FDA's own PDUFA financial reports). A broader figure — user fees as a share of the entire human-drugs / CDER program — is lower, ~66% in FY2022; the 77% is the PDUFA-program-specific number, so it is correct as stated but should not be generalized to 'the FDA' as a whole. FDA = Food and Drug Administration; CDER = Center for Drug Evaluation and Research; PDUFA reauthorized every five years (most recently 2022). The reel's inference that this funding structure means industry effectively controls approvals is Group-B framing and is not asserted here; this record documents only the funding share.
